question_text: Water is essential to life but cheap, while diamonds are not essential but expensive. Utility theory explains this by noting that prices reflect:
option_A: How long each good lasts once bought
option_B: The labor needed to produce the good
option_C: The total utility of all units consumed
option_D: The marginal utility of one more unit
explanation: Water is abundant, so the utility of one more unit is low; diamonds are scarce, so their marginal utility is high (diamond-water paradox).

question_text: Maria has 2 free hours. She values her first hour of leisure at €20 and her second at €12. She can earn €15 per hour working. How many hours should she work to maximize utility?
option_A: 1 hour, since her 2nd leisure hour is worth less than €15
option_B: 0 hours, since her 1st hour of leisure is worth more than €15
option_C: 2 hours, since earning money always beats leisure
option_D: It cannot be decided without knowing her total wealth
explanation: She should give up only the leisure hour worth less than the wage: the 2nd hour (€12 < €15). Total value is €20 + €15 = €35, the highest option.

question_text: Which marketing message most directly uses loss aversion?
option_A: 'Your free trial ends in 24 hours: don't lose access'
option_B: 'Our product is 30% cheaper than our competitors'
option_D: 'Buy now and gain access to all of our new premium features'
explanation: Framing the end of the trial as losing something already held uses loss aversion; the other messages stress price, social proof or gains.

question_text: A public health campaign wants more people to use sunscreen. Based on loss aversion, which message should work best?
option_C: 'Without sunscreen, you risk losing your healthy skin'
option_D: 'Use sunscreen to keep your skin glowing and fresh'
explanation: Stressing what people stand to lose motivates more strongly than stressing equivalent gains.

question_text: A car dealer lists a car at €40,000, then 'discounts' it to €34,000. A customer feels this is a great deal. Which concept explains this?
option_A: A nudge created through a default option in the purchase
option_B: Anchoring: the €40,000 list price sets the reference
option_C: Utility maximization by a fully rational buyer
option_D: Loss aversion toward paying the full list price
explanation: The initial list price acts as an anchor, so €34,000 is judged against €40,000 rather than against the car's actual value.

question_text: A restaurant wants guests to order more expensive wines. Based on anchoring, what should it do?
option_A: Remove all prices from the wine list entirely
option_B: Put one very expensive bottle at the top of the list
option_C: Offer a free glass of wine with every bottle
option_D: List the wines from cheapest to most expensive
explanation: A very expensive first bottle anchors guests high, so mid-to-high priced wines then seem reasonable.

question_text: A manager says: 'We have already spent €2M on this product, so we cannot stop now,' even though future revenue will not cover future costs. This reasoning is:
option_A: A correct use of return-on-investment analysis
option_B: The sunk cost fallacy: the €2M cannot be recovered
option_C: Rational protection of money already invested
option_D: Loss aversion correctly applied to company strategy
explanation: The €2M is sunk. Only future costs and revenues should decide whether to continue.

question_text: You advise a startup that has spent 18 months on a product with no market traction. The founders want to continue because of the time invested. What is the economically rational advice?
option_A: Keep going for six more months, then look at the results
option_B: Raise more funding to make up for the time already spent
option_C: Continue, because the 18 months of work must not be wasted now
option_D: Compare only future returns with future costs, then pivot or stop
explanation: The 18 months are sunk. The decision should rest only on expected future returns versus future costs.

question_text: A surgeon tells Patient A: 'This surgery has a 90% survival rate.' She tells Patient B: 'This surgery has a 10% mortality rate.' Framing research predicts:
option_A: Patient A is more likely to agree, due to the gain frame
option_B: Patient B is more likely to agree, as the risk is explicit
option_C: Both patients will respond in exactly the same way
option_D: Neither patient has enough information to make a choice
explanation: The information is identical, but the survival (gain) frame makes surgery seem less risky than the mortality (loss) frame.

question_text: A gym wants more members to renew. Which message best applies framing effects?
option_A: 'Our gym welcomed 500 new members this year'
option_B: 'New members enjoy three months for the price of two'
option_C: 'Don't lose your member discount: renew before it expires'
option_D: 'Renew your membership today for continued access to the gym'
explanation: Framing non-renewal as losing an existing discount uses a loss frame, which motivates more than a neutral or gain message.

question_text: After five reds in a row at roulette, a gambler bets on black, believing it is 'due'. This reflects:
option_A: Rational use of the true odds of the roulette wheel
option_B: Availability: recent outcomes come easily to mind
option_C: Anchoring on the first color that came up that night
option_D: Representativeness: expecting short runs to look random
explanation: The gambler expects a short sequence to resemble a random pattern (gambler's fallacy), a form of the representativeness heuristic. Each spin is independent.

question_text: A manager must choose a supplier. Supplier P had one dramatic, widely discussed failure last month. Supplier Q has a higher overall failure rate but no memorable incident. To avoid availability bias, the manager should:
option_A: Choose P, because a failure will make it more careful now
option_B: Choose Q, because P's recent failure is the most memorable
option_C: Ask colleagues which supplier they feel is the safer one
option_D: Compare the long-run failure rates of the two suppliers
explanation: Availability makes the vivid recent failure loom large. Base rates (long-run failure rates) give the correct comparison.

question_text: Prospect Theory says people evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point. Which example shows this?
option_A: A €5,000 raise disappoints someone who expected €8,000
option_B: A person prefers having more money to having less money
option_C: An investor spreads money across several different stocks
option_D: A buyer chooses the cheaper of two identical products
explanation: The raise is a gain in absolute terms but a loss relative to the expected €8,000 reference point, so it feels bad.

question_text: An investor bought a stock at €100. It is now at €80. Prospect Theory predicts the investor is most likely to:
option_A: Move the money into a broad mix of other assets
option_B: Sell at once to limit any further losses he could make on the stock
option_C: Hold the stock to avoid turning the loss into a real one
option_D: Consult a financial advisor before doing anything
explanation: In the loss domain people become risk-seeking and avoid realizing losses, so they tend to hold losing stocks.

question_text: A company sets double-sided printing as the default on all its printers. Paper use drops sharply. This works mainly through:
option_A: A rule that forbids single-sided printing at work
option_B: Anchoring on the paper use of other departments
option_C: The default effect: people keep the pre-set option
option_D: A financial penalty for printing single-sided pages
explanation: Changing a default requires effort, so most people stay with it; no option is removed or penalized.

question_text: A company wants more employees to take the stairs instead of the lift, without banning the lift. Which nudge fits best?
option_A: Close the lift except for staff with medical needs
option_B: Make the stairs visible and pleasant, with signs at the lift
option_C: Charge a small fee every time someone uses the lift
option_D: Pay a bonus to the employees who take the stairs every working day
explanation: A nudge changes the choice setting without restricting options or changing incentives; fees, closures and bonuses are not nudges.
